Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Idaho statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we say so.

Idaho property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Appeals of a property-roll assessment to the county board of equalization must be filed by the end of the county's normal business hours on the fourth Monday of June. (Idaho Code 63-501A. Taxpayer's right to appeal; source)
  • Appeals of an assessment on the subsequent property roll are due the fourth Monday of November; missed-roll appeals are due before the board adjourns at its January meeting. (Idaho Code 63-501A; source)
  • The board of equalization may consider an appeal only if it is timely filed. (Idaho Code 63-501A; source)
  • A decision of the county board of equalization may be appealed to the Board of Tax Appeals within 30 days after mailing of notice of the decision or pronouncement at hearing; the same appeal may alternatively be taken to district court in that period. (Idaho Code 63-511. Appeals from county board of equalization; source)
  • Filing an appeal does not suspend payment of property taxes pending the appeal. (Idaho Code 63-511; source)
  • The notice of appeal to the BTA is filed with the clerk/auditor of the county where the property is located; the BTA has no filing fee. (File an Appeal | Idaho Board of Tax Appeals; source)
  • Idaho property is assessed at 100% of market value less any exemptions. (Understanding Property Taxes | Idaho State Tax Commission; source)
  • If delinquent real property is not redeemed within three years from the date of delinquency, the county tax collector must make a tax deed to the county. (Idaho Code 63-1005; source)
  • Before the tax deed issues, notice of pending issue must be sent by certified mail to record owners and parties in interest no more than five months nor less than two months before the deed issues, and an affidavit of compliance recorded. (Idaho Code 63-1005(1)-(2); source)

What we could not confirm

  • Details we could not confirm on an official page are not stated.

How to sell a Idaho house when this applies to you

  1. Find out what the title company needs. For an inherited or transferred house, that usually means the recorded deed or the probate paperwork that shows who owns it today.
  2. Get a payoff for any mortgage and the amount of any unpaid property tax. Both are paid from the sale proceeds at closing.
  3. Compare offers on what you net after repairs, commissions and closing costs, not on the headline price.
  4. If you want a fast, simple closing, ask for a written cash offer. We buy houses as-is, with no repairs and no agent commission. See we buy houses in Idaho.

What a cash sale of a Idaho house looks like, step by step

People often ask what actually happens after they contact a cash buyer. Here is the usual order of events for a house in Idaho.

  1. Tell us about the property. Use the form on this page or call or text (424) 435-2326. We ask about the address, the condition and what is going on, such as a mortgage, back taxes, tenants or an estate.
  2. Get a written cash offer. We review the details and send a written offer. There is no obligation, and you can turn it down and owe us nothing.
  3. Pick your closing date. You choose the timeline. Some owners need weeks to move out, and others want to close quickly.
  4. The title company handles the paperwork. It checks ownership, pays off any mortgage and any unpaid property tax from the proceeds, and records the deed.
  5. You receive the proceeds. Our offers carry no agent commission, no fees and no closing costs to you.

Documents and information to have ready

You do not need everything below to get an offer, but each item makes the sale smoother and helps the title company work faster.

  • The deed or other proof of who owns the property today.
  • A recent mortgage statement or a payoff figure from the lender.
  • The latest property tax bill, plus any notice of unpaid or delinquent tax.
  • Homeowners association details, including dues and any unpaid assessments, if there is an association.
  • Current leases and the tenants' contact information, if the house is rented.
  • Estate paperwork, such as letters from the court, if you inherited the house.
  • A short list of known repairs. We buy as-is, but honest information avoids surprises.

Listing, selling it yourself or a cash offer: how they compare

Listing with an agent can bring a higher headline price when a house is in good shape and you have time. You pay the commission agreed in your listing contract, and you usually handle repairs, showings and the buyer's inspection requests. Closing depends on the buyer's financing.

Selling it yourself saves the listing commission but puts the marketing, the paperwork and the required Idaho disclosures on you. You still need a title company or attorney to close.

Taking a cash offer trades some of the headline price for speed and certainty. We buy as-is, so there are no repairs, no showings and no financing contingency. It tends to fit owners dealing with foreclosure pressure, an inherited house, back taxes, tenants or a move on a deadline. Compare every option on what you net after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not on the headline price.

Questions to ask before you sell in Idaho

  • Ask the title company what is owed and what the title company will need at closing.
  • Ask your lender for a written payoff figure good through your expected closing date, and ask whether there is a prepayment penalty.
  • Ask the county assessor whether a pending appeal or exemption affects the bill, and whether any exemption you receive ends when you sell.
  • If the house was inherited, ask the title company which court documents it needs before it will insure the sale.
  • If tenants live in the house, check the lease for its end date and any notice you must give.

These are general questions to start a conversation, not legal advice. Rules in Idaho change, so confirm details with the official office or a Idaho attorney or tax professional.

More questions about selling in Idaho

How fast can I close on a cash sale?

You choose the closing date within what the title company needs to clear ownership and payoffs.

Do I have to clean out or repair the house?

No. We buy houses as-is, so you do not need to make repairs before selling.

Will you buy a house that has tenants in it?

Yes. We buy rentals as-is, occupied or vacant. Tell us about the lease when you request an offer.

What if I owe more on the mortgage than the house is worth?

Tell us the payoff figure. A sale that does not cover the loan may need lender approval, so ask your lender about a short sale before you sign anything.

Can I sell an inherited house before probate is finished?

It depends on who has legal authority to sign. The title company can tell you what court paperwork it needs.

No. Requesting an offer is free and carries no obligation.

Idaho offers property tax relief for qualifying homeowners, and official sources explain the rules. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • The homestead exemption is the first $125,000 of assessed market value of the homestead or 50% of market value, whichever is less. (Idaho Code 63-602G. Homestead; source)
  • The home must be owner-occupied and the owner's primary dwelling place; the owner certifies to the county assessor that no other homestead exemption is claimed. (Idaho Code 63-602G(2); source)
  • An owner need apply only once if the owner still occupies the same homestead; the exemption is not prorated. (Idaho Code 63-602G(4)-(5); source)
  • To receive the exemption for the current tax year, application must be made by the end of business on the last business day of the year; approved applications received after the second Monday in July are granted as tax cancellations. (Idaho Code 63-602G(5); source)
  • After an owner's death the exemption continues for the year of death and the next tax year while the home remains part of the estate; the new owner must then reapply. (Idaho Code 63-602G(9); source)
  • Claiming more than one homestead exemption triggers recovery of tax up to 7 years plus a penalty equal to the recovered tax on a first instance. (Idaho Code 63-602G(6); source)

How to sell a Idaho house when this applies to you

  1. Find out what the title company needs. For an inherited or transferred house, that usually means the recorded deed or the probate paperwork that shows who owns it today.
  2. Get a payoff for any mortgage and the amount of any unpaid property tax. Both are paid from the sale proceeds at closing.
  3. Compare offers on what you net after repairs, commissions and closing costs, not on the headline price.

Idaho Homestead Exemption

  • The home must be owner-occupied and the owner's primary dwelling place; the owner certifies to the county assessor that no other homestead exemption is claimed. (Idaho Code 63-602G(2); source)
  • An owner need apply only once if the owner still occupies the same homestead; the exemption is not prorated. (Idaho Code 63-602G(4)-(5); source)

Full guide: Idaho Homestead Exemption.

What a cash sale of a Idaho house looks like, step by step

People often ask what actually happens after they contact a cash buyer. Here is the usual order of events for a house in Idaho.

  1. Tell us about the property. Use the form on this page or call or text (424) 435-2326. We ask about the address, the condition and what is going on, such as a mortgage, back taxes, tenants or an estate.
  2. Get a written cash offer. We review the details and send a written offer. There is no obligation, and you can turn it down and owe us nothing.
  3. Pick your closing date. You choose the timeline. Some owners need weeks to move out, and others want to close quickly.
  4. The title company handles the paperwork. It checks ownership, pays off any mortgage and any unpaid property tax from the proceeds, and records the deed.
  5. You receive the proceeds. Our offers carry no agent commission, no fees and no closing costs to you.

Documents and information to have ready

You do not need everything below to get an offer, but each item makes the sale smoother and helps the title company work faster.

  • The deed or other proof of who owns the property today.
  • A recent mortgage statement or a payoff figure from the lender.
  • The latest property tax bill, plus any notice of unpaid or delinquent tax.
  • Homeowners association details, including dues and any unpaid assessments, if there is an association.
  • Current leases and the tenants' contact information, if the house is rented.
  • Estate paperwork, such as letters from the court, if you inherited the house.
  • A short list of known repairs. We buy as-is, but honest information avoids surprises.

Listing, selling it yourself or a cash offer: how they compare

Listing with an agent can bring a higher headline price when a house is in good shape and you have time. You pay the commission agreed in your listing contract, and you usually handle repairs, showings and the buyer's inspection requests. Closing depends on the buyer's financing.

Selling it yourself saves the listing commission but puts the marketing, the paperwork and the required Idaho disclosures on you. You still need a title company or attorney to close.

Taking a cash offer trades some of the headline price for speed and certainty. We buy as-is, so there are no repairs, no showings and no financing contingency. It tends to fit owners dealing with foreclosure pressure, an inherited house, back taxes, tenants or a move on a deadline. Compare every option on what you net after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not on the headline price.

Questions to ask before you sell in Idaho

  • Ask the title company what is owed and what the title company will need at closing.
  • Ask your lender for a written payoff figure good through your expected closing date, and ask whether there is a prepayment penalty.
  • Ask the county assessor whether a pending appeal or exemption affects the bill, and whether any exemption you receive ends when you sell.
  • If the house was inherited, ask the title company which court documents it needs before it will insure the sale.
  • If tenants live in the house, check the lease for its end date and any notice you must give.

These are general questions to start a conversation, not legal advice. Rules in Idaho change, so confirm details with the official office or a Idaho attorney or tax professional.

More questions about selling in Idaho

How fast can I close on a cash sale?

You choose the closing date within what the title company needs to clear ownership and payoffs.

Do I have to clean out or repair the house?

No. We buy houses as-is, so you do not need to make repairs before selling.

Will you buy a house that has tenants in it?

Yes. We buy rentals as-is, occupied or vacant. Tell us about the lease when you request an offer.

What if I owe more on the mortgage than the house is worth?

Tell us the payoff figure. A sale that does not cover the loan may need lender approval, so ask your lender about a short sale before you sign anything.

Can I sell an inherited house before probate is finished?

It depends on who has legal authority to sign. The title company can tell you what court paperwork it needs.

Is there any cost to request an offer?

No. Requesting an offer is free and carries no obligation.

Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from Idaho statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we say so.

Idaho probate runs through the courts named in the sources below. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • A successor may collect personal property by affidavit 30 days after death if the probate estate, less liens and encumbrances, does not exceed $100,000. (Idaho Code 15-3-1201. Collection of personal property by affidavit; source)
  • The small-estate affidavit must state that no application for appointment of a personal representative is pending or granted in any jurisdiction. (Idaho Code 15-3-1201(a)(3); source)
  • Section 15-3-1201 addresses collection of personal property and instruments; it does not by its text transfer real property. (Idaho Code 15-3-1201; source)
  • A transfer by a fiduciary administering a decedent's estate, and a transfer from a decedent's estate, are exempt from the seller disclosure requirement. (Idaho Code 55-2505(7),(16); source)
  • A transfer from a transferor who has not occupied the property within one year and acquired it by inheritance or devise is exempt from the seller disclosure requirement. (Idaho Code 55-2505(14); source)
